newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Coffee drinkers need a mild winter in Brazil.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Coffee drinkers need a mild winter in Brazil.

text.p: A bull market is raging in world coffee.
New York futures are already at their highest since frost last hit Brazil, back in 1994. And this year's season for Brazilian frost scares hasn't begun yet.
Supply from Latin America is tight. America's stocks are at 20-year lows. So speculators are on a buying spree. And retail values are edging up again at the supermarket check-out.
In latest news, the head of Colombia's National Coffee Growers' Federation said on Tuesday that it was finding it hard to meet export commitments.
"There's very little coffee in Colombia. The federation is having enormous difficulties meeting its commitments," Jorge Cardenas told reporters.
Colombia is the number two producer after Brazil.
Prices on New York futures for the arabica type of coffee beans, mainly supplied from the Americas, have doubled this year.
And the July contract rose on Tuesday to the highest since July 1994 at $2.43 per pound in the longest sustained rally in coffee for two decades.
"The funds really started to get hold of the market," said London brokerage GNI in a commentary on Wednesday.
It noted that forecasts for cool weather in Brazil were a factor on traders' minds now, even though it is rather early in the winter there for a frost. But with stocks so low, nerves are on edge.
"A frost this year would cause chaos in world coffee markets," GNI said. "The market will therefore be incredibly sensitive to any frost threat over the course of the next 15 weeks."
The 1994 frosts cut Brazil's 1995/96 crop by some 50 percent and sent futures to near 10-year highs. Since then, coffee has ridden a rollercoaster.

In the London market, for instance, which trades the robusta type of beans, widely used in soluble and instant blends, the 1994 frost and then a drought in Brazil caused prices to quadruple to $4,140 per tonne.
But by early this year they had declined steadily to as low as $1,203. Then, as supply concerns reignited, the current new rally gathered momentum to take them back up.
Wednesday saw the London market at a new one-year high at around $1,850.

London robustas have lagged the New York arabicas in this year's rally, because robustas from Asia and Africa are in more generous supply. But some roasters (processors) may now switch to using more of the less-prized robusta coffees.
Firms that have already had to lift retail prices in recent weeks include Folgers in the United States and Douwe Egberts, owned by U.S. giant Sara Lee Corp, in Europe.
Procter & Gamble Co's Folgers has raised the price $0.80 to $3.06 since March for a 13-ounce can.

According to the New York Times, the customer is now feeling the pinch. It quoted Allon Azulai, owner of Ozzie's Coffee with shops in Brooklyn, as saying he has raised the price of a cup of coffee by a dime.
"When I first opened, I was paying less than $4 for a pound of really good coffee," Azulai said, referring to wholesale costs.
"Now it's up to $6 a pound"
A week ago, Douwe, leading roaster in the Netherlands, raised the Dutch price of a standard 250-gramme pack of coffee by 20 cents, its third rise this year.
It said in Amsterdam on Wednesday it could not rule out a further rise soon.
"We are not translating these higher world prices into an increase in shop prices at the moment but we will do if it impacts on our costs," said spokesman Joost den Haan.
Douwe Egberts, however, said it had not and would not alter the proportion of arabica and robusta beans used in its blends.
"We are a premium brand and the most important thing is to maintain the quality of our product," Den Haan said.
